strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important systems problem: combining visual-inertial SLAM robustness with dense 3D Gaussian Splatting mapping. The contribution type is best viewed as Applied/Systems rather than a purely new algorithm paper, and under that lens the integrated design is meaningful.

The system is technically well motivated: dense DROID-style correspondences, IMU preintegration, staged IMU initialization, time-varying bias estimation, loop closure, and Gaussian map updates form a coherent pipeline aimed at known failure modes of visual-only 3DGS SLAM.

Experimental coverage is broad. The paper evaluates on EuRoC, RPNG AR Table, UTMM, and FAST-LIVO2, including indoor/outdoor scenes, RGB/grayscale inputs, low frame-rate settings, motion blur, and strided-frame stress tests.

The reported tracking results are consistently strong, especially in degraded visual conditions. The recall-based strided evaluations are useful because they expose partial-track failures that ATE alone can hide.

The paper evaluates both trajectory accuracy and rendering quality, with PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS comparisons against 3DGS SLAM baselines. The rendering results generally support the claim that improved tracking and loop-consistent updates benefit map quality.
Ablations support the importance of the main engineering components: IMU fusion, loop closure, keyframe initialization, and loop-closure Gaussian updates all have measurable effects.
weaknesses: The novelty is largely an integration of known components: DROID-SLAM-style dense BA, standard IMU preintegration, staged visual-inertial initialization, pose graph loop closure, and Gaussian splatting mapping. The paper would be stronger if it more clearly isolated what is algorithmically new beyond careful systems integration.

The real-time claim is somewhat overstated. The full system runs around 7 FPS on average on an RTX 5090 for RPNG, substantially slower than HI-SLAM2 mapping, and the authors note that some IMU code is still NumPy-based. This weakens claims of deployability for AR/VR or robotics despite the strong accuracy.

Several comparisons are imperfect or hard to interpret. Some EuRoC baseline numbers are copied from prior papers rather than rerun under identical conditions, MM3DGS comparisons are incomplete due to unavailable code, and FAST-LIVO2 uses pseudo-ground truth from a LiDAR-visual-inertial method rather than independent ground truth.

The paper compares against many systems, but the baselines span different sensor assumptions and operating modes. In particular, classic VIO methods do not produce dense maps, while visual-only 3DGS methods lack IMU access; this is fair as context, but it makes the precise attribution of gains less clean.

Some technical details are underspecified or slightly inconsistent. For example, the inertial residual equations appear abbreviated, the treatment of camera-IMU extrinsics is omitted from the math, bias covariance handling is unclear, and final global BA is vision-only despite the stated tightly coupled formulation.

The system requires calibrated synchronized RGB+IMU input and a high-end GPU, does not support multi-camera or fisheye setups, and appears sensitive to extreme frame subsampling at stride 20/40. These limitations are acknowledged only briefly relative to the deployment claims.

Reproducibility is not fully convincing from the manuscript alone: the project page placeholder is empty, code release is not clearly stated, and implementation details such as optimization schedules, loss weights, and loop/BA settings are only partially specified.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: making Gaussian-splatting SLAM more robust by using IMU measurements, which is practically relevant for AR/VR, robotics, and handheld capture settings where pure visual tracking is fragile.

The system is reasonably complete, combining dense learned tracking, IMU preintegration, staged initialization, per-keyframe bias estimation, loop closure, pose-graph BA, and Gaussian map updates. Even if many pieces are inherited, the integration is nontrivial.

The experimental section covers several datasets with different sensing conditions, and reports both tracking and rendering metrics. The strided-frame evaluation is a useful stress test for visual degradation, and the paper includes ablations for IMU fusion, loop closure, keyframe initialization, and loop-closure Gaussian updates.
The reported numbers suggest clear robustness gains in some difficult regimes, especially strided EuRoC/RPNG and parts of UTMM/FAST-LIVO2, where pure visual or classical VIO baselines often fail.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited relative to the strength of the claims. The method appears largely to combine DROID-SLAM-style dense BA, standard IMU preintegration/bias modeling, existing Gaussian-splatting mapping losses, and HI-SLAM2-style pose-graph/loop-closure ideas. The paper does not convincingly isolate what is technically new beyond system integration.

The claim of robust real-time SLAM is not supported by the runtime results. The full tracking+GS system runs at roughly 4-11 FPS on an RTX 5090, with an average of 7.09 FPS on RPNG, while the input is 30 FPS. The text says future CUDA optimization is needed, which weakens the current real-time claim.

The baseline protocol raises fairness and reproducibility concerns. Some EuRoC numbers are copied from prior papers, some are reproduced, MM3DGS-SLAM is only partially compared because code is unavailable, and FAST-LIVO2 uses FAST-LIVO2-generated pseudo ground truth while also evaluating against classical VIO systems. These choices make the claimed state-of-the-art comparison less convincing.

The paper overstates superiority. On EuRoC, gains over HI-SLAM2 are small on average, and the method is not uniformly best across sequences. On FAST-LIVO2, HI-SLAM2 is very close after final BA, and on some sequences better. At high stride settings, the method also degrades severely, yet the discussion presents robustness rather broadly.

Important implementation details are underspecified for reproducibility: weighting between visual and inertial terms, covariance construction, optimization schedules, calibration assumptions, bias priors, failure criteria, and exact baseline configurations are not described in enough detail to independently verify the results.

The ablations are too coarse to substantiate the main algorithmic claims. Removing all IMU fusion, all loop closure, or all keyframe initialization does not disentangle the contributions of staged initialization, time-varying bias modeling, Jacobian preintegration correction, dense correspondence initialization, and Gaussian update mechanics.

The evaluation of mapping quality is tied to keyframe selection and estimated poses, but the paper gives limited analysis of how pose errors versus Gaussian optimization affect rendering metrics. Qualitative results are sparse and do not show failure cases or map consistency under loop closure in a diagnostic way.

Several claims are rhetorically stronger than the evidence, such as attributing ORB-SLAM3 performance to handcrafted features and non-differentiable components without controlled experiments, or claiming tight visual-inertial coupling while the optional final global BA is vision-only because inertial constraints supposedly offer limited refinement benefit.

The manuscript has presentation issues that hurt confidence: formatting glitches in equations/tables, inconsistent terminology, typos such as the loss term notation, dense tables that are hard to parse, and a relatively thin limitations section that omits calibration sensitivity, IMU noise/bias sensitivity, rolling shutter, synchronization, and compute/memory limits.

strengths: The manuscript presents a timely and useful visual-inertial 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM system. Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, the work is best assessed as an Applied/Systems contribution: the main value is a complete real-time-capable SLAM pipeline that integrates dense learned tracking, IMU preintegration, staged IMU initialization, bias estimation, loop closure, and Gaussian map maintenance.

The experimental evidence is broad and generally convincing. Results cover four datasets with different sensing rates and conditions, including EuRoC, RPNG AR Table, UTMM, and FAST-LIVO2, and compare against visual SLAM, visual-inertial SLAM, and 3DGS-SLAM baselines. The method is consistently strong in tracking accuracy, recall under strided-frame stress tests, and rendering quality.

The ablation studies support the main design choices. Removing IMU fusion, loop closure, keyframe IMU initialization, or loop-closure Gaussian updates substantially degrades tracking or rendering, which makes the system-level contribution more credible.

The paper is technically sound overall. The visual-inertial objective, IMU preintegration with bias correction, staged initialization, pose-graph loop closure, and anchored Gaussian updates are plausible and well aligned with established SLAM practice while addressing a real weakness of purely visual 3DGS SLAM methods.

The paper is clearly written and well organized, with useful implementation details and supplemental tables. The authors also report online results before final global BA/color refinement, which makes the comparison more meaningful for SLAM use cases.
weaknesses: The novelty is mostly integrative rather than fundamentally algorithmic. Many components are inherited from DROID-SLAM, standard IMU preintegration/VIO, pose-graph BA, and prior Gaussian SLAM systems. The paper would be stronger if it more sharply isolated what is conceptually new beyond engineering a strong combination.

The runtime claim is only partially convincing. The full tracking plus Gaussian mapping speed is around 7 FPS on an RTX 5090 for RPNG, below real-time camera rates and slower than HI-SLAM2. The paper acknowledges unoptimized NumPy code, but the current evidence weakens the claim of robust real-time operation on practical hardware.

Some comparisons are imperfect or hard to interpret. Several baseline numbers are copied from prior papers or unavailable for all sequences, MM3DGS-SLAM is not directly comparable due to missing released RGB+IMU support, and FAST-LIVO2 uses pseudo ground truth from a LiDAR-visual-inertial system rather than independent ground truth.

The robustness study is useful but partly synthetic. Strided-frame evaluation simulates frame drops and high-speed motion, but it does not fully replace evaluation on naturally degraded synchronized camera/IMU sequences with blur, rolling shutter, dropped frames, or calibration errors.

The paper leaves some reproducibility gaps. It gives many hyperparameters, but does not clearly state code/data release status, exact baseline tuning fairness, calibration assumptions, or sensitivity to camera-IMU extrinsics and timestamp offsets. These details matter for visual-inertial SLAM systems.

The limitation discussion is somewhat short. It mentions lack of multi-camera/fisheye support and high-end GPU requirements, but does not deeply discuss failure modes such as dynamic scenes, poor IMU calibration, severe rolling shutter, long-term map growth, memory usage, or deployment on embedded AR/robotics platforms.
